title: House and Choir
premise: Beatrix Eriksen returns to her family's decaying manor to bury her twin sister, only to learn the body in the coffin isn't her sister — and the excavation crew digging the new foundation has broken into a door sealed from the inside. Beneath the house lies a chapel where the household's vanished servants, and generations of Eriksens, still sing a song that grants the household its uncanny prosperity. The song demands a final verse, and it has chosen Beatrix's voice to complete it. To save her sister — held in the choir as the verse's anchor — Beatrix must learn the song without ever singing along, and end it by unmaking the door from her side, sacrificing her own belonging to free the choir. In the end she buries her sister for real and leaves the house silent, hollow, and hers no longer.
about_author: O. M. Galloway is the pen name of a former church organist who spent a decade restoring liturgical manuscripts in northern coastal towns. Their fiction explores what communities ask of the people who keep them singing.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body in the Coffin
chapters.summary: Beatrix arrives at Eriksen House for her twin's funeral and discovers the corpse's teeth are wrong — her sister had a chipped canine. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: grief curdling into denial, establishing her identity as the twin who never believed in the family's old stories.

chapters.title: What the Excavation Found
chapters.summary: The foundation crew breaks through into a stone stairwell ending at a door scarred by claw marks on the inside. That night Beatrix hears humming through the floorboards. POV: Beatrix, with a brief crew foreman interlude. Emotional beat: dread replacing denial; the house stops pretending to be empty.

chapters.title: Aunt Maren's Ledger
chapters.summary: Beatrix finds a household ledger listing servants paid in 'verse-counts' instead of wages, each entry ending when the singer's name is struck through. Aunt Maren, lucid for once, warns her: never answer when the house calls your name. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the past becomes evidence; loyalty to family begins to feel like complicity.

chapters.title: The Choir Below
chapters.summary: Following the humming, Beatrix reaches the sealed door and hears her sister's unmistakable voice among many, singing a song with no final verse. She speaks her sister's name; the singing stops; every candle in the house gutters at once. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: hope weaponized — her sister is alive, and the house knows she knows.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: The house begins teaching her the song in dreams, each night one verse longer, each morning another staff member gone or strangely serene. Beatrix transcribes the verses to learn the structure without singing. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: seduction — the song is beautiful, and belonging has never felt so easy.

chapters.title: Maren Sings
chapters.summary: Aunt Maren, who once refused the final verse sixty years ago, is found at the open door, mid-hymn, young again and empty-eyed. She is drawn below to join the choir. POV: Beatrix, closing with Maren's fragmentary perspective. Emotional beat: horror of the cost — refusal only delays the choice, and the house collects.

chapters.title: The Terms of Belonging
chapters.summary: Beatrix confronts the house itself through the ledger, which now writes back: her sister lives as long as the song remains unfinished, and the verse requires a twin's voice given freely. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the trap closes — power is offered, not forced, and that is what makes it corruption.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: Beatrix masters the final verse in silence, discovering it is not an ending but a binding — the last verse is the door. She prepares to sing it wrong, to break the song rather than complete it, knowing it may kill her sister. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: resolve; loyalty to her sister finally outweighs loyalty to blood and house.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Beatrix descends, opens the door from outside, and faces the choir — her sister at its center, the household's dead arranged in rows. She sings the final verse backwards, unbinding it; the chapel collapses inward as the choir, freed, disperses like breath. She drags her sister out as the door seals itself again — from the outside. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: climax and sacrifice — she loses the house's power and nearly her sister.

chapters.title: A Quiet Inheritance
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Beatrix buries her sister's actual body and sells the house to a developer with no interest in foundations. The new owners report the halls sing when it rains. Beatrix, deaf in one ear since that night, does not believe — and never will again. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; truth survived, belonging forfeited, and the song endures without her.
